newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Police break up protests in two Argentine provinces.
newsitem.headline: Police break up protests in two Argentine provinces.

text.p: Riot police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up protests in two Argentine provinces on Tuesday, one by laid-off sugar workers in the north and another by street hawkers in Buenos Aires province.

Local media reports said at least 50 people were injured when paramilitary police broke up a roadblock in the poor northwestern province of Jujuy by 200 sugar workers and their families demanding new jobs. About 4,000 of them have been laid off by the Ledesma sugar company in recent years.
Police gave them 10 minutes to clear National Highway 34, then waded in with truncheons, tear gas and rubber bullets.

In La Plata, capital of Argentina's most populous region, Buenos Aires Province, 60 hawkers protesting a clampdown on illegal stalls by authorities clashed with police, who responded with rubber bullets and tear gas. Police told national television that three officers had been injured and a handful of hawkers arrested.

Riot police in armoured cars then began patroling the city centre and arrested students in the city's university for allegedly joining in the protest, while a group of hawkers burst into a television station and occupied the studios.
Just a day earlier, riots broke out in the central city of Mendoza; and 20 people were hurt in clashes between police and unionists protesting against industry privatisation plans.

There have been numerous roadblocks against Argentina's high unemployment rate, currently more than 17 percent, in recent weeks -- as far apart as Neuquen in the far south and Highway 34 in Salta province, next door to Jujuy.

While Argentina's economy has found new stability since President Carlos Menem came to power in 1989, joblessness has risen rapidly, forcing thousands to seek a precarious living by setting up often illegal street stalls.

Unions blame Menem's privatisations and economic reforms for the dearth of jobs and held three general strikes last year. One radical union leader, Carlos "the Dog" Santillan of the Jujuy state workers' union, said of Tuesday's incident:
"They were unemployed people demanding a response from the national or provincial government. Unfortunately the response was repression."
Menem, whose Peronist Party faces tough mid-term Congress elections later this year, blamed the unrest on what he termed "presubversive gymnastics" encouraged by the political opposition.
